Egress allowlisting, since exfiltration needs an outbound channel and rendering a model-supplied URL is sufficient. Idempotency keys and rate limits so retries do not double-charge. Hard caps on steps and spend. Dry-run modes for high-stakes flows. And full audit logging of every action with its trigger, because reconstructing and reversing an incident is impossible without it. Ask first whether untrusted content and sensitive capability need to be in the same session at all, since separating them eliminates a class of attack rather than mitigating it.

sections.heading: Recurring design questions
sections.body:
Structured and unstructured together: route rather than force one mechanism. Analytical questions go to text-to-SQL with schema retrieval, column descriptions, and verified example queries, executed read-only with row limits, query surfaced for transparency, model narrating returned rows rather than inventing numbers. Prose goes to RAG. Support combining both, since 'why did my bill increase' needs the policy and the actual charges. Evaluate the SQL path with execution accuracy, not string similarity.

Multi-tenancy: cross-tenant leakage is a security incident, so isolation lives in the data path and never in a prompt. Separate namespaces for the strongest guarantee and cleanest deletion, or a shared index with mandatory filters enforced in a data access layer rather than trusting call sites, with adversarial tests. Then resource isolation, since one tenant's agent loop should not exhaust capacity, and one sending very long contexts consumes disproportionate KV memory. Per-tenant cost attribution from day one, and deletion that propagates to indexes, caches, logs, and traces.

Scarce labels: ship a heuristic or zero-shot baseline first, because a system in production generates the feedback that produces labels. Then active learning to spend annotation budget on uncertain examples, weak supervision via labeling functions, transfer learning, and LLM labeling with sampled human verification. Protect the evaluation set absolutely: it must be human-labeled even when training labels are noisy, or you lose the ability to tell whether anything is improving.

Rule-based to ML migration: respect the rules, since they encode undocumented edge cases and give you both a baseline and a label source. Shadow the model, then focus on disagreements with expert adjudication, which measures readiness credibly and produces high-value labels. Take over incrementally by segment or confidence band, with rules retained as fallback and permanently for hard legal or policy constraints that should not become probabilistic.

Multiple languages: quality will be uneven because pretraining data is, so measure per language rather than reporting an average. Tokenization matters concretely, since non-Latin scripts consume two to four times more tokens, raising cost and eating context. Translate-to-English is a fallback, not a default, since it compounds errors and mangles entities. Design in tiers with explicit graceful degradation, and tell users which languages work best rather than silently serving bad output.

sections.heading: The three months question
sections.body:
Asked constantly in one form or another: you have limited time and no ML infrastructure, what do you do?

Do not build the platform first. That means designing abstractions for requirements you do not understand and arriving with infrastructure and nothing shipped, which also costs the credibility needed to fund phase two.

Pick one use case that is genuinely valuable, narrow enough to finish, and tolerant of errors, preferring internal or assistive over automated customer-facing, since early blast radius is what kills programs. Minimize what you own: hosted APIs rather than self-hosted serving, retrieval rather than fine-tuning, off-the-shelf components. Invest properly in exactly two things from day one, an evaluation harness and tracing, because they make every subsequent iteration measurable and both are painful to retrofit.

Shipping is how you learn what infrastructure you actually need: where your data is broken, what your latency budget truly is, which failure modes matter. That should drive what you build second.

And handle the organizational side: instrument feedback capture at launch, set the expectation that version one is a starting point improved with real data, and pick something with a measurable outcome so you can demonstrate value and earn the next mandate. Defer fine-tuning, since without data and evaluation you cannot even tell whether it would help.

One more scenario worth rehearsing: you are asked to build something you believe will not work. Neither refuse nor comply silently. Name the specific failure mode with evidence, propose a cheap experiment that resolves the disagreement empirically, and distinguish the risk type, since a quality or ROI concern is a legitimate business tradeoff the product owner can accept, while a safety, privacy, or legal risk needs explicit escalation and sign-off. If the decision stands, build it properly and instrument it well, and write down the assumption up front so the result becomes shared learning rather than an argument about who was right.
